provenance.rightsStatus: Seventeen sources are reference-only and no prose was adapted from any of them; two (Dallimore et al. 2019 and Kirschner et al. 2018) are CC BY 4.0 and are still synthesised rather than quoted. All wording, the analogy, the worked example and the question bank are original.
provenance.transformation: Built from primary experimental and meta-analytic literature plus three IES/WWC practice guides, each verified at source through the ERIC API, Crossref, the publishers' own pages, or full-text extraction of the published article. The machine-generated draft supplied nothing but the topic title and was discarded entirely. The lesson is organised around a single argument the sources jointly support - that strategy effectiveness is conditional on learner prior knowledge, knowledge type and phase of learning - rather than as a catalogue of methods. Hattie's effect sizes are deliberately not used as magnitudes anywhere; the published statistical criticism of them is taught instead. Topics owned by neighbouring lessons (backward design, cognitive load mechanics, study strategies, the minimal-guidance debate) are referenced and handed off, not re-taught.

title: Differentiated Instruction
in30Seconds: Differentiated instruction adjusts teaching in response to what students actually know. Carol Ann Tomlinson's framework names four things a teacher can vary - content, process, product, and learning environment - and three student traits to vary them for: readiness, interest, and learning profile. Pre-assessment is the engine: you adapt to measured readiness, not to a label, a hunch, or a learning style. The framework is popular, and the evidence for it as a package is thinner than that popularity suggests.
whyItMatters: Every class contains students who are already fluent with today's objective and students who are missing its prerequisite. Differentiation is the vocabulary that teacher-preparation programs, evaluation rubrics, and school improvement plans use for that problem, so you will be asked to do it and asked to defend it. Knowing the framework lets you plan adaptations that keep the same learning goal for everyone rather than quietly lowering it for some. Knowing the evidence lets you argue about it honestly, which matters more than it sounds: the underlying moves are better supported than the branded package, and a differentiation claim in an interview or a classroom observation is far stronger when you can name which assessment drove which grouping decision.
learningObjectives: Define differentiated instruction as responsive teaching and distinguish it from an organizational or scheduling change.
Explain how content, process, product, and learning environment are adjusted in response to readiness, interest, and learning profile.
Distinguish assessed readiness from ability, labels, and prior placement, and explain why pre-assessment is the engine of the approach.
Distinguish flexible grouping from fixed ability grouping and summarize the mixed research record on grouping.
Apply tiering, fading scaffolds, and choice to a scenario while holding the learning goal constant.
Evaluate the evidence base for differentiation honestly, separating the packaged approach from its component practices.

collegeVersion.heading: Responsive teaching, defined
collegeVersion.body: Carol Ann Tomlinson and her colleagues describe differentiation as a pedagogical change rather than an organizational one. It is not a timetable, a program, or a way of sorting students into different rooms. It is a set of decisions a teacher makes about curriculum and instruction inside one mixed classroom: proactively modifying curricula, teaching methods, resources, learning activities and the products students make, because the learners in front of you vary. Practitioners usually compress the framework into four adjustable elements and three student traits. The elements are content (what students work with, and how they get access to it), process (the activities through which they make sense of it), product (how they show what they now know), and learning environment (how the room, the groupings, and the routines are arranged). The traits are readiness, interest, and learning profile. The review's first hallmark is that effective differentiation is proactive rather than reactive, and that distinction carries more weight than it sounds. A teacher who plans one lesson for everyone and improvises when it visibly fails is not differentiating; the review argues that this kind of on-the-spot tinkering with one-size-fits-all instruction is too small a modification to meet the range in a real class. Differentiation is planned before the lesson, on evidence gathered before the lesson.

collegeVersion.heading: Readiness is measured, not assumed
collegeVersion.body: Readiness is the trait most often misread, and getting it right is what separates differentiation from streaming with friendlier vocabulary. Readiness is not ability, not intelligence, and not a judgment about how far a student can eventually go. It is where one student stands right now with respect to one objective, and it moves from unit to unit and skill to skill: the student who needs heavy support with proportional reasoning may need none at all with data displays three weeks later. Tomlinson's review grounds readiness in Vygotsky's zone of proximal development and in the broader claim that learning happens at moderate challenge - beyond what a student can already do alone, but reachable with support. Because readiness is that specific and that unstable, it has to be measured rather than inferred. Pre-assessment is the engine of the whole approach: a short quiz, a sorting task, a writing sample, or simply the end-of-unit problems handed out at the start. It converts 'I think some of them already know this' into a decision you can defend to a student, a parent, or an observer. The federal evidence here is instructive in two directions at once. The What Works Clearinghouse practice guide on response to intervention in primary reading recommends exactly this - provide differentiated reading instruction for all students based on assessments of their current reading levels - and then rates the level of evidence for that recommendation as low, resting largely on correlational work. The companion guide on using student achievement data to support instructional decision making puts every one of its five recommendations, including the ongoing data cycle itself, at the lowest evidence rating the Clearinghouse assigns. The panels recommend the practice anyway. A well-taught version of this topic says both halves out loud.

collegeVersion.heading: Flexible grouping, and the tracking question
collegeVersion.body: Flexible grouping means groups that form, do a specific job, and dissolve. Membership is set by current evidence about one skill, and it is expected to change when the next check says it should. Across a single unit a student might sit in a readiness group on Monday, an interest group on Wednesday, and a deliberately mixed group on Friday. Fixed ability grouping - tracking, streaming, setting - is the opposite: a placement made once and carried for a term or a year, often across subjects. Collapsing the two is the most common way differentiation goes wrong in practice, and the research record here is genuinely mixed rather than settled. A second-order meta-analysis synthesizing roughly a century of grouping research found positive achievement effects for within-class grouping (g of about 0.19 to 0.30), for cross-grade subject grouping (g of about 0.26), and for special grouping of gifted students (g of about 0.37), but effectively nothing for between-class grouping (g of about 0.04 to 0.06) - and the effects did not differ for high-, medium-, or low-ability students. A meta-analysis of differentiation practices in primary education points the other way on one important sub-question: homogeneous ability grouping, whether between or within classes, showed a small negative effect for low-ability students and no effect for anyone else, and the authors conclude that grouping alone does not amount to differentiated instruction. Both findings can stand. The syntheses cover different populations, outcomes, and comparison conditions. What they agree on is the part that matters for practice: the act of sorting students is not what produces gains. What changes inside the group - the materials, the pace, the complexity of the task, the amount of teacher attention - is what produces them. Tomlinson's review reaches the same conclusion from the other direction, reporting meta-analytic evidence for small within-class groups and then insisting that gains are largest when materials actually differ between those groups rather than being handed out identically.

collegeVersion.heading: The four moves that do the work
collegeVersion.body: Most of differentiation in practice reduces to four moves. Tiering builds parallel versions of one assignment: the same essential understanding and the same standard of quality, with differences in complexity, abstraction, open-endedness, or built-in support. Scaffolding supplies temporary help - a worked example, a sentence frame, a partly completed organizer, a teacher sitting with a small group. The research literature defines scaffolding by three features, and only the first is obvious: contingency, meaning the support is adjusted to what this learner actually does; fading, meaning it is withdrawn over time; and transfer of responsibility, meaning the student ends up doing the work. Support that is never faded fails the definition. It is not a scaffold but a permanent accommodation, and it quietly lowers the goal for the students who receive it. Choice - choice boards, task menus, product options - differentiates by interest and by working preference while holding the objective fixed; a student who can explain photosynthesis in a diagram, a paragraph, or a two-minute recording is being assessed on the same understanding either way. Varied pacing treats time as a resource rather than a constant, which the review flags as a chronic failure: instruction is typically pitched at the middle or the top and paced for one group, leaving the rest either frustrated or idle. Every one of these moves holds the learning goal still and moves the route.

collegeVersion.heading: What the evidence actually supports
collegeVersion.body: Differentiation is far more popular than its evidence base, and a lesson that hides this does students no favours. The strongest positive synthesis is in elementary literacy: across 18 studies of teacher-led differentiation, the overall weighted mean effect was g = +0.13, with 88 percent of individual estimates positive and considerable variation by domain - letter-word reading around +0.20, writing around +0.96. That is a real effect, and it is small. The authors also report an alarming lack of information about how teachers decided what to differentiate and for whom, which is a striking gap in studies of a practice whose whole logic is decision-making. At secondary level the picture is thinner still: a systematic review covering a decade found only 12 usable empirical studies, mostly showing small to moderate positive effects, and concluded that severe knowledge gaps remain and that convincing conclusions about effectiveness cannot yet be drawn. That review also documents why the effect sizes are hard to read. Studies count wildly different things as differentiation - ability grouping, tiering, individualization, mastery learning, heterogeneous grouping, flipped classrooms - and they typically lean on research teams to build the materials and coach the teachers, so what was tested is not what a teacher does unaided on a Wednesday. Implementation fidelity is the recurring weak point, and it cuts both ways: in the correlational study behind the federal reading recommendation, students of teachers who implemented the differentiation program with greater fidelity showed greater reading growth. The honest summary is this. Differentiation as a branded package has thin support. Its ingredients - pre-assessment and formative feedback, scaffolding with fading, small-group instruction targeted by data, tasks pitched at moderate challenge - carry better-established evidence on their own. Teach the ingredients, and treat the package as a useful organizing vocabulary rather than a proven intervention.

collegeVersion.heading: The learning-profile problem
collegeVersion.body: Tomlinson's review defines learning profile as a student's preferred mode of learning, shaped by factors it lists as learning style, intelligence preference, gender, and culture. One part of that definition has aged badly, and pretending otherwise is not defensible. The claim that instruction produces more learning when its modality is matched to a student's stated preference - the meshing hypothesis - has been tested with the design capable of showing it, and the crossover interaction it predicts essentially does not appear; a later direct experiment with adults found no relationship between auditory or visual-word preference and comprehension when instruction was matched to preference. So do not administer a VARK-style inventory, label students visual or auditory, and route instruction accordingly. That is not differentiation, and it is not supported. What survives from learning profile is a narrower and more defensible set of things: student interest, meaningful choice, the cultural and linguistic knowledge students bring to a task, and preferences about working conditions - alone or with others, in discussion or in silence, in one long block or several short ones. Those are claims about the conditions under which a person works well, not claims that information enters certain brains better through certain sensory channels. Tomlinson's own review, to its credit, cautions that no particular approach to learning is superior to another. The cognitivism topic in this subject handles the full learning-styles debunk; the point to carry away here is only that differentiation and style-matching are different things, and the second one is not evidence.

collegeVersion.heading: Where Universal Design for Learning fits
collegeVersion.body: Universal Design for Learning, developed by CAST, is a related but distinct framework and it is worth being able to tell them apart in a seminar. UDL organizes instructional design around multiple means of engagement, representation, and action and expression, built into goals, methods, materials, assessments, and the learning environment from the outset so that fewer individual adaptations are needed afterwards. It designs options up front, for anyone who walks through the door. Differentiation adapts for the particular learners in this room, on evidence gathered about them. A common shorthand says UDL is proactive and differentiation is reactive; avoid it, because Tomlinson's first hallmark is that differentiation is proactive too. The cleaner distinction is who the design is for - all learners in general, or these learners in particular - and when the information arrives. The two are routinely used together, and the inclusive-teaching topic covers UDL in depth.

vocabulary.definition: Where a particular student stands right now with respect to a particular objective, established by assessment rather than by a general judgment about ability.
A check given before teaching begins, used to find out what students already know so that tasks and groups can be set on evidence rather than guesswork.
Forming and dissolving small groups repeatedly across a unit, with membership set by current evidence about one skill instead of fixed for the term.
Sorting students into separate classes or streams by measured attainment, with placement typically fixed for a term or a year and often applied across subjects.
A set of parallel versions of one assignment, all aimed at the same essential understanding, differing in complexity, abstraction, or built-in support.
Temporary support that lets a learner do something they could not yet do alone, adjusted to that learner's responses and intended to be withdrawn.
The deliberate withdrawal of support as a learner takes over more of the task; without it, help becomes a permanent substitute for the goal.
A menu of alternative tasks or products, all pointed at the same objective, from which students select according to interest or working preference.
In Tomlinson's framework, a student's preferred way of working, which the review attributes to learning style, intelligence preference, gender, and culture.
How closely a practice is actually carried out as designed when it reaches a real classroom, and a recurring weak point in studies of this approach.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Imagine a teacher has to get thirty people across the same river. Reaching the far bank is not negotiable - that is the learning goal, and it is the same for everyone. But some people can wade straight across, some need stepping stones, and a few could swim it twice and be bored waiting. Differentiated instruction means finding out who is who before anyone gets wet, handing stepping stones to the people who need them, and then taking the stones away as soon as a person can wade without them. Teachers get this wrong in two ways: guessing who needs stones instead of checking, and letting some people stop halfway across because the bank was quietly moved closer for them.
eli10.analogy: Think of a doctor's office. Everyone in the waiting room has the same goal - get healthy - but nobody expects the same prescription, and nobody gets a prescription before an examination. The examination is pre-assessment, the prescription is the tiered task, and the follow-up appointment is the next check that decides whether the treatment changes or stops.
eli10.analogyLimits: The analogy breaks in two places. A doctor sees patients one at a time; a teacher works with thirty at once and can realistically run only a handful of versions, which is exactly why differentiation is hard to implement well and why studies of it so often find weak fidelity. And medicine has trial evidence for specific prescriptions, while differentiation as a named package does not - its individual ingredients are better supported than the whole.

workedExample: A seventh-grade teacher opens a unit on proportional reasoning with a six-item pre-assessment on Monday. Of 28 students, 6 solve multi-step proportion problems correctly, 15 handle simple unit rates but stall on scaling, and 7 cannot yet write a ratio in simplest form. The objective stays identical for all three groups: use proportional relationships to solve multi-step problems. The task is tiered. The 7 work with the teacher on ratio notation using a partly completed table. The 15 get the same word problems with a worked example on the reverse. The 6 get problems with an extra unknown and no worked example. On Wednesday an exit ticket regroups everyone: 4 of the 7 have the notation and move up, so 3 remain. The pre-assessment set the groups; the exit ticket dissolved them.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating differentiation as learning styles - giving a VARK-style inventory, labeling students visual, auditory, or kinesthetic, and matching instruction to the label.
commonMistakes.correction: This is the meshing hypothesis, and adequately designed studies do not find the crossover interaction it predicts; a direct test found no relationship between modality preference and comprehension under matched instruction. Tomlinson's own definition of learning profile does name learning style as a component, which is the weakest part of the framework and should not be taught as practice. Differentiate on assessed readiness, on interest, and on working conditions - not on a sensory label.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating differentiation as workload adjustment - fewer problems for the students who are struggling, extra problems for the students who are ahead.
commonMistakes.correction: Tiering varies complexity, abstraction, and support while holding the essential understanding and the standard of quality constant. Cutting the number of items lowers exposure without changing difficulty; adding items rewards speed with more of the same. Both leave the actual learning goal untouched, and the first quietly removes it from the students who most need practice.

commonMistakes.mistake: Grouping by a label or a prior placement - IEP status, gifted identification, last year's reading level - and calling the result differentiation.
commonMistakes.correction: Readiness is specific to the objective and changes across a term, so groups have to be re-formed on current evidence about the skill being taught. A placement fixed in September has stopped responding to anything. This is also the line between flexible grouping and tracking: between-class ability grouping shows effectively no achievement benefit in the meta-analytic record, and one primary-grade meta-analysis found a small negative effect of homogeneous grouping for low-ability students.

commonMistakes.mistake: Skipping pre-assessment and differentiating from impressions of who seems strong or weak.
commonMistakes.correction: Without a pre-assessment there is no readiness data, only a ranking of students by confidence, compliance, or last term's grade. Pre-assessment is what makes the adaptation defensible and what makes regrouping possible; the federal practice guide recommendation is specifically to differentiate on assessments of students' current levels, not on professional impression.

commonMistakes.mistake: Presenting differentiated instruction as a proven, evidence-based practice.
commonMistakes.correction: The best positive synthesis, in elementary literacy, reports an overall weighted mean of g = +0.13 across 18 studies; the secondary-level review found only 12 usable studies and concluded that severe knowledge gaps remain. Say instead that the component moves - pre-assessment, scaffolding with fading, small-group instruction targeted by data, tasks at moderate challenge - have better individual support than the packaged approach does.

compareContrast.distinction: Flexible groups are formed on current evidence about one skill and dissolved when the next check says so; tracking is a placement made once and carried for a term or year, often across subjects. The meta-analytic record is broadly positive for within-class grouping and effectively null for between-class grouping, though one primary-grade synthesis found a small negative effect of homogeneous grouping for low-attaining students.

Readiness is a measured, task-specific, temporary state relative to one objective; ability is a general trait attribution. Differentiation is defensible only when it responds to the first, because the second turns adaptation into a permanent expectation.

A tiered task keeps the essential understanding and the quality standard fixed and varies complexity, abstraction, or support. Adjusting how many items a student completes changes volume, not challenge, and does not adapt the learning.

UDL designs multiple means of engagement, representation, and action and expression into goals, methods, and materials up front for all learners; differentiation adapts for the particular learners assessed in one class. They are complementary, and both are planned rather than improvised.

A scaffold is contingent on the learner's response and is faded as responsibility transfers to the student. Support that is never withdrawn no longer meets the definition and functions as a lowered goal.

keyTakeaway: Differentiation adapts content, process, product, and learning environment to assessed readiness and to student interest while holding the learning goal fixed; its component moves, especially pre-assessment and scaffolds that are faded, are better supported by evidence than the packaged approach that names them.

questionBank.prompt: In Tomlinson's framework, which four classroom elements can a teacher differentiate?
options: Content, process, product, and learning environment
Curriculum, assessment, homework, and grading
Readiness, interest, learning profile, and motivation
Objectives, standards, pacing guides, and report cards
questionBank.explanation: The framework separates what a teacher can adjust - content, process, product, and learning environment - from the student traits those adjustments respond to. Readiness, interest, and learning profile are the traits, not the elements, which makes the third option a deliberate confusion of the two lists. Grading, standards, and report cards are not part of the framework's adjustable elements.
questionBank.skill: Recalling the structure of the differentiation framework

questionBank.prompt: A teacher gives students a style inventory, labels them visual, auditory, or kinesthetic, and delivers each group's instruction in its matching modality. What is wrong with this?
options: Nothing - this is the standard application of learning profile
It should be done after the unit rather than before it
It uses too few categories to capture real learner variation
It relies on the meshing hypothesis, which adequately designed studies do not support
questionBank.explanation: Matching instruction to a stated modality preference is the meshing hypothesis, and the crossover interaction it predicts does not appear in studies designed to detect it; a direct experiment also found no relationship between auditory or visual-word preference and comprehension under matched instruction. The problem is not the number of categories or the timing - adding more style categories or moving the inventory later would not rescue an unsupported claim.
questionBank.skill: Separating differentiation from learning-styles matching

questionBank.prompt: In September a teacher sorts a class into three reading groups using last year's end-of-year scores and keeps the same membership all year. Why does this fail as differentiation?
options: The groups are too large to allow individual attention
Readiness is task-specific and changes, so grouping must be flexible and driven by current assessment
Reading is a subject where students should never be grouped
Three groups is too few to cover the range in a typical class
questionBank.explanation: Readiness describes where a student stands on a particular objective right now, so a placement fixed in September on last year's data has stopped responding to anything. Flexible grouping re-forms membership on current evidence about a specific skill. Group size and the number of groups are practical questions, not the defining fault here, and grouping for reading is not itself prohibited - fixing it for a year is the problem.
questionBank.skill: Distinguishing flexible grouping from fixed ability grouping

questionBank.prompt: Which statement best characterizes the current research evidence on differentiated instruction?
options: Meta-analyses show large, consistent achievement gains across subjects and age groups
There is no evidence of any kind that differentiation affects achievement
Effects are typically small, the study base is limited and heterogeneous, and implementation fidelity is often weak
The evidence is strong at secondary level but has never been studied in primary grades
questionBank.explanation: An elementary literacy meta-analysis found an overall weighted mean of g = +0.13 across 18 studies, and a secondary-level systematic review located only 12 usable studies and concluded that severe knowledge gaps remain. Effects exist but are small, what counts as differentiation varies widely between studies, and implementation is frequently propped up by research teams. The first option overstates the evidence, the second denies findings that do exist, and the fourth inverts the actual pattern - the primary-grade literature is the better developed one.
questionBank.skill: Evaluating the strength of an education evidence base

questionBank.prompt: A pre-assessment shows wide variation in a class starting persuasive writing. Which plan is a properly tiered task rather than a change in workload?
options: Struggling writers write three paragraphs; confident writers write six on the same prompt
All groups argue a position from evidence, with one group given a source set and an organizer, another given the sources unorganized, and a third finding and evaluating their own sources
Struggling writers complete a grammar worksheet while confident writers draft the essay
Confident writers draft the essay and then tutor the struggling writers, who do not draft one
questionBank.explanation: Tiering keeps the essential understanding constant - here, arguing a position from evidence - and varies complexity and support. Only the second option does that. The first varies length, which is workload, not challenge. The third and fourth remove the actual objective from the students who most need practice at it, substituting a worksheet or a tutoring role for the writing itself.
questionBank.skill: Designing a tiered task that holds the learning goal constant

quickCheck.prompt: In Tomlinson's framework, which four classroom elements can a teacher differentiate?
options: Content, process, product, and learning environment
Curriculum, assessment, homework, and grading
Readiness, interest, learning profile, and motivation
Objectives, standards, pacing guides, and report cards
quickCheck.explanation: The framework separates what a teacher can adjust - content, process, product, and learning environment - from the student traits those adjustments respond to. Readiness, interest, and learning profile are the traits, not the elements, which makes the third option a deliberate confusion of the two lists. Grading, standards, and report cards are not part of the framework's adjustable elements.
quickCheck.skill: Recalling the structure of the differentiation framework

quickCheck.prompt: A teacher gives students a style inventory, labels them visual, auditory, or kinesthetic, and delivers each group's instruction in its matching modality. What is wrong with this?
options: Nothing - this is the standard application of learning profile
It should be done after the unit rather than before it
It uses too few categories to capture real learner variation
It relies on the meshing hypothesis, which adequately designed studies do not support
quickCheck.explanation: Matching instruction to a stated modality preference is the meshing hypothesis, and the crossover interaction it predicts does not appear in studies designed to detect it; a direct experiment also found no relationship between auditory or visual-word preference and comprehension under matched instruction. The problem is not the number of categories or the timing - adding more style categories or moving the inventory later would not rescue an unsupported claim.
quickCheck.skill: Separating differentiation from learning-styles matching

quickCheck.prompt: In September a teacher sorts a class into three reading groups using last year's end-of-year scores and keeps the same membership all year. Why does this fail as differentiation?
options: The groups are too large to allow individual attention
Readiness is task-specific and changes, so grouping must be flexible and driven by current assessment
Reading is a subject where students should never be grouped
Three groups is too few to cover the range in a typical class

title: Formative Versus Summative Assessment
in30Seconds: The same ten-question quiz can be formative or summative. What decides is not the instrument but the use made of the evidence: an assessment is formative when something actually changes because of what it showed, and summative when it records where a learner stood at an end point. Michael Scriven coined the pair in 1967 for judging curricula; Benjamin Bloom moved it onto student learning two years later. Every other term in this unit hangs off that distinction.
whyItMatters: Assessment is where students first meet the gap between what a course says it values and what it actually rewards. Teacher preparation programs, licensure exams and school improvement plans all use this vocabulary, and they use it loosely: districts buy products labeled formative that are nothing of the kind. Getting the distinction right protects you from that. It also transfers. Anyone who trains, coaches, reviews code or supervises a clinical rotation faces the same question about whether an evaluation exists to improve the work or to certify it, and the same temptation to attach a score to advice that would have worked better without one.
learningObjectives: Define formative and summative assessment in terms of the purpose and use of the evidence rather than the type of instrument.
Explain how Scriven's 1967 distinction for curriculum evaluation became Bloom's distinction for evaluating student learning.
Distinguish assessment for learning, assessment as learning and assessment of learning, and place diagnostic, interim and benchmark assessment among them.
Apply the purpose test to classify a real assessment scenario, including cases where the same instrument is used both ways.
Analyze why feedback effects vary in direction, and why attaching a grade to a comment tends to blunt the comment.
Evaluate the evidence behind popular claims about the size of formative assessment's effect on achievement.

collegeVersion.heading: Purpose, not instrument
collegeVersion.body:
Michael Scriven introduced the pair of terms in 1967, and not about students at all. He was writing about how to evaluate curricula, and he separated two roles evaluation might play: one in the ongoing improvement of a curriculum while it was still being developed, and one that let administrators decide whether the finished curriculum represented a sufficient advance on the available alternatives to justify adopting it. He proposed calling those roles formative and summative.

Two years later Benjamin Bloom moved the distinction onto student learning. He acknowledged the traditional role of tests in judging and classifying students, and set against it a use of formative evaluation that provides feedback and correctives at each stage of the teaching-learning process - brief tests used by teachers and students as aids to learning. Bloom then added the sentence everything downstream depends on: such tests may be graded and used in the judging function, but formative evaluation is much more effective when it is separated from grading and used primarily as an aid to teaching.

Read those origins carefully and the most common student error dissolves. Neither Scriven nor Bloom made formative a property of an instrument. A test is not formative; a use is. Dylan Wiliam states the criterion sharply: assessments are formative if and only if something is contingent on their outcome and the information is actually used to alter what would have happened without it. An exit ticket nobody reads is summative in effect - a record and nothing more. A state accountability test whose results genuinely reshape next summer's teacher workshops has been used formatively, however high its stakes were for the students who sat it.

So the distinction is not about timing, format, formality, or low stakes. Wiliam describes a continuum of cycle lengths instead: short-cycle within a single lesson, five seconds to an hour; medium-cycle between lessons, a day to two weeks; long-cycle between instructional units, four weeks to a year or more. What makes any of them formative is not the length of the loop, where it happens, who runs it, or even who responds. It is that evidence is evoked, interpreted in terms of learning needs, and used to adjust.

collegeVersion.heading: For learning, as learning, of learning
collegeVersion.body:
A second vocabulary sits alongside the first and is often mistaken for a synonym. Writing for Manitoba Education and the Western and Northern Canadian Protocol, Lorna Earl and Steven Katz set out three purposes of classroom assessment.

Assessment for learning gives teachers information they use to modify and differentiate teaching. It asks not only what students know but how, when and whether they apply it, and it feeds both instructional adjustment and feedback to students.

Assessment as learning puts the student in the driver's seat. Its object is metacognition: students monitoring their own understanding, judging their work against criteria, and adjusting their strategies. Earl and Katz note that systematic assessment as learning has historically been rare, and it is the category most schools underuse. The 2018 revision of the Council of Chief State School Officers' definition makes the same move, extending the goal of the process to supporting students to become self-directed learners.

Assessment of learning is summative: it confirms what students know and can do and produces statements of proficiency that other people - the next teacher, an admissions office, a licensing board - will rely on.

Two cautions. Some writers use only two categories and fold assessment as learning into assessment for learning, so the three-way split is a convention, not a law. More importantly, Earl and Katz argue that it is very difficult and sometimes impossible to serve three assessment purposes at once. An assessment designed to let students expose their confusion without penalty is not the same artifact as one designed to survive scrutiny as a proficiency claim, and trying to do both usually means doing the first one badly.

collegeVersion.heading: The neighboring labels
collegeVersion.body:
The FAST SCASS collaborative of state assessment directors published a paper for the express purpose of untangling the labels, and each one names something real.

Summative assessment provides information about the level of student, school or program success at an end point in time, after instruction concludes. Its results serve evaluative judgment, inferences about mastery, grades, and accountability requirements.

Interim assessment - also called benchmark, common, or quarterly assessment - covers tests administered periodically through the year to serve some mix of three functions: predicting performance on a later high-stakes test, evaluating programs, and supplying teachers with individual student data. Many such products were marketed as being formative assessments in themselves. FAST SCASS quotes Margaret Heritage's diagnosis that the core problem is the false but widespread assumption that formative assessment is a particular kind of measurement instrument rather than a process. Their own verdict is blunter: interim tests give periodic snapshots, but because they are not proximate to learning as it develops they do not inform ongoing teaching, and at the time of writing there was no meaningful evidence that they enhance student learning.

Diagnostic assessment is a procedure detailed enough to indicate which specific subskills or pieces of enabling knowledge a student does and does not possess. It answers what is not being learned, rather than whether learning is happening. Because it is time-intensive it is normally reserved for students who are not progressing, and it feeds the formative process when results arrive fast enough to act on.

Three further labels round out the set. Curriculum-embedded assessment is built into the materials or activities, so students are never told to stop and take a test. Universal screening is a brief measure given to everyone two or three times a year to flag students who may be at risk. Progress monitoring is a short measure repeated weekly or biweekly to track growth, usually with alternate forms.

Notice that every one of these is defined by an instrument, a population, or a schedule - not by a purpose. That is why each can be used formatively or summatively, and why the purpose test still has to be applied on top of the label. FAST SCASS makes the point about curriculum-embedded work explicitly: it is more likely to be formative when it is not graded, and once it enters the grading process the only thing distinguishing it from any other summative assessment is how smoothly it was blended into the lesson.

collegeVersion.heading: Feedback is not automatically good
collegeVersion.body:
The engine of formative assessment is supposed to be feedback, so it matters that feedback is not a reliably positive intervention. Avraham Kluger and Angelo DeNisi's 1996 meta-analysis pooled 607 effect sizes from 23,663 observations. The average effect was positive and moderate, d = .41. But over one third of the feedback interventions decreased performance - a substantial minority of cases in which telling people how they were doing made them worse.

Their explanation, Feedback Intervention Theory, is that feedback works by directing attention, and that its effectiveness falls as attention moves up a hierarchy from the task toward the self. Feedback that says this paragraph has no evidence in it points at the work. Feedback that says you are a careless writer, or simply 71 percent, points at the person. The second kind recruits ego defense, and ego defense does not revise paragraphs.

This is the mechanism behind the oldest practical rule in the field. Bloom said in 1969 that formative evaluation is much more effective when separated from grading. Ruth Butler tested it in 1988, giving fifth- and sixth-grade classes numerical grades, individual comments, or both, and framing the contrast as task-involving versus ego-involving evaluation. The reading that has stuck in teaching-center guidance is that adding a score to a comment removes the benefit of the comment. Black and Wiliam reached the same conclusion from the wider literature: pupils given only marks or grades do not benefit from the feedback, which improves learning when it gives specific guidance on strengths and weaknesses, preferably without any overall marks.

The operational consequence is simple. If you want a comment to do work, protect it from the grade - withhold the score until the student has responded, require a revision before releasing it, or do not score the piece at all. Writing both on the same page and hoping the student reads the left column is, on this evidence, wishful.

collegeVersion.heading: What good formative practice actually contains
collegeVersion.body:
The 2018 FAST SCASS definition calls formative assessment a planned, ongoing process used by all students and teachers during learning and teaching to elicit and use evidence of student learning, improve understanding of intended disciplinary learning outcomes, and support students in becoming self-directed learners. It names five practices that must be integrated: clarifying learning goals and success criteria within a broader progression of learning; eliciting and analyzing evidence of student thinking; engaging in self-assessment and peer feedback; providing actionable feedback; and using that evidence and feedback to move learning forward.

Strip that to the three parts that fail most often.

First, success criteria stated in advance. Students cannot judge their own work against a standard they have not been shown, and a teacher who has not written the criterion down will grade by impression. It is also what separates feedback from opinion.

Second, evidence from every student. A question answered by the three students who raise their hands tells you about three students. Wiliam's illustration is a multiple-choice question about thesis statements where every student holds up a lettered card, so the teacher reads the whole room at once and knows who chose what. He calls the resulting instant a moment of contingency: the point at which instruction can actually change direction. Contrast it with the class discussion that feels productive and yields no readable evidence about anyone.

Third, a decision that follows. This is what the definition is really about, and the part routinely skipped. Evidence that produces no change in what happens next was not formative, however carefully it was gathered.

The word planned in the 2018 definition is doing deliberate work here. FAST SCASS argues that a teacher who appears to be adjusting on the fly is often enacting one of several plans prepared beforehand - anticipating the likely misconceptions, writing the question that will surface them, and deciding in advance what each pattern of answers will trigger. Improvisation of that quality is rehearsed.

collegeVersion.heading: How strong is the evidence?
collegeVersion.body:
You will meet a number attached to this topic, and you should handle it carefully. In their 1998 Phi Delta Kappan article Inside the Black Box, Paul Black and Dylan Wiliam wrote that typical effect sizes of the formative assessment experiments were between 0.4 and 0.7, larger than most found for educational interventions, and that improved formative assessment helps low achievers most. That sentence became the most-quoted claim in classroom assessment, repeated in textbooks and district slide decks as though it were a measured constant.

It is not one. Neal Kingston and Brooke Nash reviewed more than 300 K-12 studies of formative assessment and found only 13 reporting enough information to compute an effect size. From the 42 independent effect sizes those studies yielded, a random-effects model gave a weighted mean of 0.20, with estimates of 0.32 in English language arts, 0.17 in mathematics and 0.09 in science. Their conclusion was that the commonly claimed figure is not supported by the existing research base, and that the base itself is too thin.

Randy Bennett's critical review attacks the object rather than the estimate. He concluded that formative assessment does not yet name a well-defined set of artifacts or practices, that the breadth of the definitions in use permits implementations with wildly different outcomes, and that the magnitude of the common quantitative claims is suspect because it traces to sources that are untraceable, flawed, dated or unpublished. If the treatment is not well defined, an average effect size for it means little.

The original authors have qualified their own case. Writing in 2006, Wiliam said his own reading of the research suggested medium-cycle formative assessment had shown only modest impact, and that the studies which did show impact tended to be those that changed teachers' day-to-day and minute-to-minute practice. Federal guidance is similarly restrained: the 2009 IES practice guide on using student achievement data assigns a Low level of evidence to all five of its recommendations. Low, the panel is careful to say, means it did not identify a body of research demonstrating effects on achievement - not that the practice is unimportant.

So hold this position. The mechanism is well motivated: eliciting evidence, interpreting it, and acting on it is how teaching becomes responsive rather than scheduled. The size of the effect is unsettled, depends heavily on what was implemented, and should not be quoted as a fixed number.

vocabulary.definition: The process of eliciting evidence of learning and using it to change what a teacher or student does next; the label attaches to the use made of the evidence, not to the instrument.
An assessment whose results are used to record or certify the level a student, class or program has reached at an end point, typically after instruction has concluded.
Evidence gathered so that a teacher can modify and differentiate instruction and give students feedback that advances their work.
The use of assessment to build metacognition, with students monitoring their own understanding against criteria and adjusting their own strategies.
The summative purpose: confirming what students know and can do, and producing statements of proficiency that other people will act on.
A detailed evidence-gathering procedure that identifies which specific subskills or pieces of enabling knowledge a student is missing, normally reserved for students who are not progressing.
A test given periodically through the school year, also called benchmark or quarterly, used to predict later test performance, evaluate programs, or report individual student data.
The stated features of acceptable work, shared with students in advance so that both teacher and learner can judge a performance against the same standard.
The instant in a lesson at which evidence from students has been read and instruction can genuinely change direction as a result.
Comment that tells a learner what is strong, what is weak and what to do next, directed at the work rather than at the person.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Imagine two ways of weighing yourself. If you step on the scale, look at the number, and change what you eat this week, the weighing changed something. If you step on the scale on the last day of a study so a researcher can write the number down, the weighing recorded something. It is the same scale and the same body. What differs is what happens next. School assessments work exactly this way. A quiz is formative when the teacher or the student does something different because of the answers. The same quiz is summative when its only job is to go in the grade book. So the useful question is never whether something is a formative assessment. The useful question is who is going to change what they do because of this, and how soon.
eli10.analogy: Formative assessment is tasting the soup while you cook. Summative assessment is the diner tasting the soup after it is served. Same spoon, same soup, different job. The cook can still add salt; the diner can only deliver a verdict, and the verdict arrives too late to rescue that bowl.
eli10.analogyLimits: The analogy hides three things. The cook tastes for herself, but the strongest versions of formative assessment put the spoon in the student's hand and teach them to judge their own work. Soup is not discouraged by criticism and students are; a third of feedback interventions in one large review made performance worse. And the diner's verdict can be formative for the next batch, which is the whole point: it is the use, not the moment, that decides the label.

workedExample: Two teachers give the same ten-item quiz on Tuesday. Ms Okafor collects the papers, scores them out of ten, records the scores, and hands them back Wednesday with the marks circled. Her class moves on to the next section as planned. Mr Bhatt writes no score. He tallies which item each student missed and finds that nineteen of his twenty-six students missed item 7 in the same way, subtracting before distributing. He cancels Wednesday's planned lesson, reteaches distribution for fifteen minutes, and ends the period with a two-item re-check. He returns the quizzes with a written comment and no number, because a number would have crowded the comment out. Same instrument, same students, same day. Ms Okafor ran a summative assessment: the evidence became a record. Mr Bhatt ran a formative one: the evidence changed the next lesson. Note what Mr Bhatt needed and Ms Okafor did not - a response from every student, an interpretation of those responses in terms of learning needs, and a decision that actually followed.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating formative and summative as categories of test, so that quizzes and exit tickets are filed as formative and exams as summative.
commonMistakes.correction: They are categories of use. The same quiz is formative if its results change the next lesson and summative if they only get recorded. Classify the decision that follows, not the paper.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling any low-stakes or ungraded activity formative, even when nobody looks at the results.
commonMistakes.correction: Being ungraded is not sufficient. An assessment is formative only if something is contingent on its outcome and the information actually alters what would otherwise have happened.

commonMistakes.mistake: Accepting a vendor's or district's label - treating a quarterly benchmark product as formative because it is sold that way.
commonMistakes.correction: Interim and benchmark tests are a separate category defined by their schedule and function. They inform ongoing teaching only when results arrive in time to change instruction and someone changes it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Quoting an effect of 0.4 to 0.7 standard deviations as the established benefit of formative assessment.
commonMistakes.correction: That range comes from a 1998 summary article. A later meta-analysis found a weighted mean of about 0.20 from the few studies with usable data, and critics have shown the original figures trace to sources that cannot be checked.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming more feedback is always better, so long as it is delivered kindly.
commonMistakes.correction: In the largest meta-analysis of feedback interventions, over a third lowered performance. Feedback aimed at the person rather than the task is the failure mode, and a grade written beside a comment tends to pull attention toward the person.

compareContrast.distinction: Formative use changes what happens next for these learners; summative use records where they stood. The same instrument, and even the same administration, can be put to either use.
Both are formative in purpose, but for learning positions the teacher as the one who acts on the evidence, while as learning trains the student to monitor and adjust their own work.

Diagnostic work is fine-grained and targeted at students who are stuck, identifying which subskill is missing. Interim tests are broad periodic snapshots of the whole cohort, better at prediction and reporting than at telling a teacher what to do on Thursday.

A grade summarizes the person's standing; descriptive feedback describes the work and what to do to it. Delivered together, the grade tends to win the student's attention and the feedback's benefit is lost.

keyTakeaway: Formative and summative name what you do with the evidence, not kinds of tests. If nothing changed because of what an assessment showed, it was not formative - whatever it was called, however low the stakes, and however carefully the data was collected.

questionBank.prompt: When Michael Scriven proposed the terms formative and summative in 1967, what were the two roles he was distinguishing?
options: Two ways of reporting an individual student's report card grade.
A role in the ongoing improvement of a curriculum, and a role in deciding whether to adopt the finished curriculum.
Two levels of rigor in teacher licensure examinations.
Two statistical methods for estimating the reliability of a test.
questionBank.explanation: Scriven was writing about curriculum evaluation, not students. He separated evaluation that contributes to improving a curriculum while it is being developed from evaluation that lets administrators judge whether the finished curriculum is enough of an advance to justify adopting it, and named those roles formative and summative. Bloom applied the same distinction to student learning two years later; report cards, licensure and reliability estimation had nothing to do with the original proposal.
questionBank.skill: Recall the historical origin of the formative/summative distinction.

questionBank.prompt: What does it mean to say that formative assessment is a process rather than an instrument?
options: Only observations and conversations can be formative; written tests never can.
Whether an assessment is formative depends on how the evidence is elicited and used to change teaching or learning, so the same test can serve either purpose.
Formative assessment must be administered at fixed intervals throughout the school year.
An assessment is formative whenever it is ungraded, regardless of whether anyone acts on the results.
questionBank.explanation: The FAST SCASS adopted a process definition precisely as a counter to treating formative assessment as a kind of instrument, and Bloom noted from the start that the same tests could be used either way. Written tests can absolutely be used formatively, so A is wrong. Fixed intervals describe interim assessment, not formative assessment, so C is wrong. D is the most tempting error: being ungraded helps, but without a decision that follows, nothing was formative.
questionBank.skill: Explain the purpose criterion that defines formative assessment.

questionBank.prompt: A district buys a quarterly benchmark test marketed as a formative assessment. Score reports reach teachers three weeks after each administration, once the unit has ended, and no instructional change follows. How is this best classified?
options: Formative, because the test is given during the year rather than at its end.
Formative, because the publisher designed it to inform instruction.
Diagnostic, because the report breaks results down by subskill.
An interim assessment being used summatively, because nothing was contingent on the results.
questionBank.explanation: The instrument is an interim or benchmark test - periodic, cohort-wide, predictive and evaluative in function. Its use here is summative, because the evidence produced no change in what happened next, which is the criterion for formative use. Being mid-year does not make an assessment formative, a vendor's label does not decide the question, and a subskill breakdown alone does not make a broad periodic test a diagnostic procedure.
questionBank.skill: Apply the purpose criterion to classify a real assessment scenario.

questionBank.prompt: A teacher writes a detailed comment on every essay and also records a letter grade at the top of the page. Based on the feedback research, what is the most defensible prediction?
options: The grade will strengthen the comment, because students treat graded work more seriously.
The comment will work just as well with the grade as without it, since feedback effects are consistent across conditions.
The grade is likely to blunt the comment, because evaluation that draws attention to the self rather than the task tends to weaken feedback effects.
Neither will affect performance, because feedback interventions have no average effect.
questionBank.explanation: Kluger and DeNisi found that feedback becomes less effective as attention moves from the task toward the self, and Butler's comparison of grades, comments, and grades plus comments is the classroom demonstration of that mechanism. Black and Wiliam advise giving guidance on strengths and weaknesses preferably without any overall mark. Option D misstates the meta-analysis, whose average effect was positive (d = .41) even though over a third of interventions lowered performance.
questionBank.skill: Analyze why combining a grade with feedback weakens the feedback.

questionBank.prompt: A student teacher writes that formative assessment 'raises achievement by 0.4 to 0.7 standard deviations.' What is the most accurate correction?
options: That range comes from Black and Wiliam's 1998 summary article; later work has not confirmed it, a meta-analysis found a weighted mean near 0.20 from the few studies with usable data, and critics argue the original figures trace to sources that cannot be checked.
The range is accurate but applies only to mathematics classrooms.
The range is far too low; recent meta-analyses report effects above 1.0 standard deviations.
Effect sizes are not used in education research, so the sentence is meaningless.
questionBank.explanation: The 0.4 to 0.7 figure originates in Inside the Black Box (1998). Kingston and Nash found only 13 of more than 300 studies had usable data and obtained a weighted mean of 0.20, and Bennett argued the common quantitative claims derive from untraceable, flawed, dated or unpublished sources. Kingston and Nash reported mathematics as one of the weaker subject estimates, not a special case where the range holds, so B is wrong; no credible synthesis reports above 1.0; and effect sizes are used routinely in education research.
questionBank.skill: Evaluate the evidential standing of a widely repeated quantitative claim.
